News.title: Exact dates to book off in May 2026 to turn 8 days of annual leave into 20 days off
News.content:
HOLIDAY lovers can bag a mega break next month, and it won’t cost them their entire annual leave allowance.

With a bit of smart planning, Brits can stretch just eight days of leave into 20 days off work.



The best part is that it all centres around May, one of the best months of the year for sunshine, staycations and cheap getaways.



The first UK bank holiday of the month lands on Monday, May 4, while the second comes later in the month, on Monday, May 25.

By booking just four days after each bank holiday, you can unlock two separate nine-day breaks.

For the first stretch, book off Tuesday, May 5 through to Friday, May 8.

This will give you nine days off in a row when combined with the bank holiday and surrounding weekends.



Then do the same again later in the month by booking Tuesday, May 26 to Friday, May 29.

That second block will also land you another nine-day break for the price of just four days’ leave.

Altogether, that’s 18 days off using only eight days of annual leave.

Throw in the weekend of Saturday, May 16 and Sunday, May 17, and you have a whopping 20 days off in the month.



Many workers could see almost a three-week break away from the office.

It’s the perfect chance to plan a long-haul holiday, multiple mini breaks, or simply enjoy more time at home without burning through your allowance.

With another bank holiday still to come in August, savvy workers have plenty more chances to make the most of their time off before the year is out.

News.title: Trump warns ‘we may have to start bombing again’ as he issues new 4-day ultimatum to Iran & vows to keep Hormuz blockade
News.content:
DONALD Trump has warned the US will resume its brutal bombing campaign in Iran if peace is not reached in four days – and vowed to keep the Strait of Hormuz blockade “in full force”.

Tehran has meanwhile declared that the vital 24-mile wide waterway will remain “fully open” for the remainder of the two-week ceasefire, as tracking data showed a fleet of oil tankers sail through.





But Trump has threatened to start “dropping bombs” if the regime doesn’t renege on their nuclear ambitions and accept Washington’s terms by Wednesday.

The US president has appeared optimistic that a deal will be reached, telling reporters aboard Air Force One that he had received some “pretty good news” on the state of a deal.

He added: “It seems to be going very well in the Middle East with Iran.

“You’ll hear about. I just think it’s something that should happen. It’s something that only makes sense to happen. And I think it will.”

The White House is considering releasing $20billion (£14.75bn) in frozen Iranian assets to get negotiations over the line after last weekend’s peace talks fell flat.

Crunch peace negotiations between both sides are ongoing with a three-page plan reportedly being mulled over before a second round of talks in Pakistan this weekend.

Hostilities between the warring nations appeared to have cooled after Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi declared the Strait of Hormuz would be opened.



Trump celebrated the breakthrough on Truth Social, writing: “IRAN HAS JUST ANNOUNCED THAT THE STRAIT OF IRAN IS FULLY OPEN AND READY FOR FULL PASSAGE. THANK YOU!”

He called it a “A GREAT AND BRILLIANT DAY FOR THE WORLD!” and claimed: “Iran has agreed to never close the Strait of Hormuz again.

“It will no longer be used as a weapon against the World!”

But hours later, regime Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf warned that the key trade route “will not remain open” if the US naval siege persists after another source branded it “a violation of the ceasefire”.

The US blockade only applies to Iranian ships, those that have visited Iranian ports and vessels carrying sanctioned oil.



Commercial ships not linked to the regime should now be able to pass through the waterway but many are hesitant after weeks of war.

Trump said today that “most of the points are already negotiated” for the peace agreement, so the process of closing the deal “should go very quickly”.

Direct peace talks reportedly fell through between the US and Iran last weekend when Tehran refused to stop enriching uranium.

Trump has meanwhile blasted America’s Nato allies once again, telling them to “stay away” from the Strait of Hormuz after it called to offer help.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He wrote: “I TOLD THEM TO STAY AWAY, UNLESS THEY JUST WANT TO LOAD UP THEIR SHIPS WITH OIL.



“They were useless when needed, a Paper Tiger!”

News.title: Iran’s top negotiator hits out at Trump’s ceasefire claims as crooked terror leaders claim US will never have nuke dust
News.content:
IRAN’S top negotiator has slammed Donald Trump’s ceasefire claims as leaders vow the US will never get hold of the nuclear dust.

In a post on social media, Mohammed-Bagher Ghalibaf wrote: “The President of the United States made seven claims in one hour, all seven of which are false.”





Earlier today, Trump emphatically declared that Iran will never shut the Strait of Hormuz again.

“They did not win the war with these lies, and they certainly will not get anywhere in negotiations either,” Ghalibaf wrote.

“With the continuation of the blockage, the Strait of Hormuz will not remain open.”

He continued: “Passage through the Strait of Hormuz shall be conducted on the ‘designated route’ and with ‘Iranian authorisation’.



“The open or closed status of the strait and the regulations governing it shall be determined by the field, not by social networks.”

This comes after Trump declared the Strait of Hormuz “fully open”, but not for Iranian ships.

As it stands the US blockade only applies to Iranian ships that have visited Iranian ports, as well as vessels carrying sanctioned oil.

The US president said the American naval blockade on Iran will “remain in full force” until a permanent deal is struck with Tehran.



Celebrating the breakthrough on Truth Social, Trump wrote: “IRAN HAS JUST ANNOUNCED THAT THE STRAIT OF IRAN IS FULLY OPEN AND READY FOR FULL PASSAGE. THANK YOU!”

“Iran has agreed to never close the Strait of Hormuz again,” Trump added.

“It will no longer be used as a weapon against the World.”

Iran’s foreign minister issued a similar declaration, stating the waterway was “completely open” for the rest of the temporary ceasefire.

Abbas Aragchi said the decision to open the shipping lane came after Israel agreed to stop blitzing Lebanon with a ten-day temporary ceasefire that started on Thursday night.



The US president also said on Thursday night that Iran had “agreed not to have a nuclear weapon” and that talks over a lasting agreement will “probably” take place this weekend.

“The U.S.A will get all Nuclear ‘Dust,’ created by our great B2 Bombers – No money will exchange hands in any way, shape or form,” Trump said.

Speaking about Iran’s supply of enriched Uranium, Trump said: “We’re going to get it together. We’re going to go in with Iran, at a nice leisurely pace, and go down and start excavating with big machinery.

“We’ll bring it back to the United States.”

The White House is said to even be considering a $20billion (£14.75bn) deal to entice Tehran to give up its entire stockpile of enriched Uranium.



Peace talks previously broke down due to Iran’s refusal to abandon its nuclear ambitions.

According to reports, Washington has now asked to be sent all of Iran’s nuclear material via ship.

In response Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said: “Iran’s enriched uranium is not going to be transferred anywhere.”

Instead, it would only consider “blending it down” inside the country – into dust form.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A rumoured compromise under discussion would see some of the highly enriched uranium shipped to a country which is not the US.



Crunch talks are now ongoing between the sides with US Vice President JD Vance expected to lead a second round of talks in Pakistan this weekend.

News.title: EasyJet cabin crew terrified they might be ‘furloughed’ if flights are axed amid fuel shortage
News.content:
EASYJET is among airlines which could run out of aviation fuel by the end of May – leaving cabin crew terrified they might be “furloughed”.

Holidaymakers could suffer flight heartache, with carriers’ global networks facing chaos due to the crisis in the Middle East.



No-frills EasyJet expects to lose £560m for the first half of the 2026 financial year due to the ongoing crisis – and the workforce is worried about layoffs.



One staff member claimed bosses opened up about the extent of the airline’s woes during a flight back from Marrakech in Morocco.

He told colleagues: “We are meant to be running out of jet fuel by the end of May. Possible furloughs will come into effect at the company, and unpaid leave will become a thing this summer if the situation doesn’t change in the Middle East.

“If the situation lasts, the UK is heading for a recession. If the Strait of Hormuz doesn’t open soon, it will be a loss for the medium haul. Prior to the war, more than 100 ships were passing through with fuel. Now, there’s four if we’re lucky.”

EasyJet last night moved to allay staff fears by saying furlough had not been discussed.



One worker told The Sun: “It’s like covid all over again – the idea we could lose our jobs, even temporarily, is terrifying. The airline is in a good position, and hopefully the worst possible scenario won’t become a reality. It would be a kick in the teeth to hard working crew.”

The airline has written to employees setting out the carrier’s dicey future.

The update, shared with The Sun, said of the monster financial losses: “This reflects a more challenging external environment, including increased fuel costs linked to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, a deeply concerning humanitarian situation as well as an economic one.”

The airline went on: “The current environment brings continued uncertainty. Fuel price volatility and a shorter booking curve are impacting forward visibility, and competitive pressures remain in some markets.”



And staff were told: “We are already taking action, including adjusting capacity where routes are not performing, reviewing pricing to reflect higher fuel costs, improving operational efficiency in how we fly, and reducing weight where possible.”

EasyJet’s grim forecast to staff came as it publicly updated the markets, revealing how fuel costs were up by £25m in the last month alone.

EasyJet chief executive Kenton Jarvis said talk of having to cancel flights was pure speculation.

He added: “We have visibility to the middle of May and we have no concerns.”

But Ryanair’s Michael O’Leary admitted of the fuel crisis: “Nobody is willing to give us any assurances into June or July. But if there’s a risk to 10% or 20% of the fuel supply in June, July or August, then we and all other airlines would have to start looking at cancelling some flights or taking some capacity out.”



EasyJet told The Sun last night that a crew member’s conversation with bosses – prompting his outburst to colleagues over furlough – does not represent its view.

The airline moved to assure staff that it has “no plans for furlough” and unpaid leave is a normal process open to crew throughout the year.

The carrier said: “All our flights continue to operate as normal, we have seen no disruption to fuel supply and we remain in close contact with our fuel suppliers and airports. EasyJet’s financial strength means we are well positioned to navigate these geopolitical challenges.”

News.title: Wife-killer Robert Brown who bludgeoned Joanna Simpson set to make a fresh bid for freedom next week
News.content:
WIFE-killer Robert Brown is to make a fresh bid for freedom next week.

The ex-British Airways pilot, 62 — who bludgeoned Joanna Simpson with a hammer — will face a parole hearing for the first time since The Sun helped block his release.





He was jailed for 26 years in 2011 after admitting manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility.

He had been scheduled for automatic early release in November 2023 over the killing in Windsor, Berks, in 2010 after serving half his term.

But the then-Justice Secretary Alex Chalk stepped in to prevent him from being able to walk free without any assessment.



It came after The Sun launched its Justice For Joanna campaign.

A Parole Board hearing will be held in private next Thursday and Friday after a request for a public one was rejected in 2024.

The Board said at the time it wanted “to ensure that the hearing will be fair and achieve the right result”.

Joanna’s mum Diana Parkes and friend Hetti Barkworth-Nanton said: “We knew this day was coming.



“This was exactly what we expected.

“Joanna was a kind and loving daughter, mother and friend.

“She was taken from us in the most brutal way and is deeply missed every day.”

News.title: Rachel Reeves gives strongest hint yet she’ll ditch fuel duty hike this year in bid to ‘keep costs down’ for families
News.content:
RACHEL Reeves insists her priority is “keeping costs down” for struggling families in the strongest sign yet she will abandon a fuel duty hike this year.

The Chancellor vows she will do “everything in my power” to protect households and businesses by averting an increase in pump prices amid the energy price shock.





Her intervention came as forecourt costs across the country dropped slightly but diesel is still just below 191p per litre and petrol is at 157p per litre, the RAC said.

Energy costs have soared since the US airstrikes on Iran led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, stopping oil and gas supplies from leaving the region until yesterday (Fri).

But the Chancellor last night told The Sun: “I know families are worried about what’s happening in the world right now. About what it means at the pumps, at the tills and for people’s pockets.

“People are struggling. As Chancellor, my priority is keeping costs down for families and businesses – and I’m angry that they will feel the financial fallout of a war that’s not their fault.

“But those costs are real, and I want to reassure the British people that I get it – I will do everything in my power to protect them.

“The world is uncertain right now. Working people deserve a Chancellor who listens and acts. I am doing both.”

The 5p fuel duty discount is due to expire from September when it will gradually be phased out fully by March next year.

It was brought in under the Tories in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine back in 2022 to help counter high prices.



Both petrol and diesel have begun to drop for the first time since before the war started.

But petrol is still 25p more a litre and diesel is up by 48p per litre since the start of the conflict, the RAC said.

Simon Williams, from the RAC, said: “After 46 days of rising prices, the cost of both petrol and diesel across the country has finally begun to drop very slightly.

“After record rises, drivers will be relieved to finally see prices going the other way.

“While we’re a long way from a return to the prices we had at the start of the conflict, there’s now a glimmer of light at the end of the tunnel.”



Any decision by the Chancellor to scrap the fuel duty hike will cost the public purse around £2.6 billion.

She is under intense pressure balancing the public finances with the International Monetary Fund downgrading the UK’s growth prospects this year and next.

She is grappling with demands to fill a £28 billion black hole in the defence budget and also reduce the ballooning welfare budget.

Reeves said it would have been better to carry on with diplomatic efforts to ensure Iran didn’t have a nuclear weapon rather than going down the military channel.

News.title: We’ve got to move faster and spend more, says armed forces minister Al Carns as he blasts dithering defence plans
News.content:
ARMED forces minister Al Carns has taken aim at fellow ­ministers for dithering over defence plans.

The ex-Special Boat Service colonel said: “We need investment decisions to be made. We’ve got to move faster and spend more.”





And he warned Britain needs to re-arm — fast.

He said: “We’ve got to fill the stocks.

“We’ve got to be ready to go in three to five years, so by 2029.”

It comes amid claims Chancellor Rachel Reeves is blocking more cash for the MoD despite a £28billion budget black hole.

The PM’s ten-year defence spending plan has been stalled for months.

Mr Carns is the most decorated MP since World War Two.

Yet he is not part of Labour’s long-delayed Defence Investment Plan (DIP) that decides which weapons will be funded in future.

He said: “What we need is investment decisions to be made so we can enhance our lethality and capability.”



A Government spokesman said it was investing “over £270billion in defence across this Parliament” and its DIP will “deliver the best kit into the hands of our Armed Forces, ensuring they are ready to face future threats”.

News.title: Moment recycling plant burns in huge blaze as 27 fire engines battle inferno and crews still fight 2 days on
News.content:
THIS is the moment firefighters battle a huge blaze as it violently rips through a recycling unit.

Dramatic footage shows crews dousing towering flames as thick black smoke billows into the sky as the fire tears through the site.





Fire engines surround the building while firefighters work frantically to contain the blaze.

At its height, 27 fire engines were called in to tackle the flames at Wiser Recycling in Thetford, Norfolk.

They received the call saying that the site was ablaze just after 7pm on Thursday.

Businesses in Brunel Way, where the recycling firm is based, were evacuated as the fire took hold.



Firefighters worked through the night to bring the situation under control, battling what was described as a “significant” blaze.

In an update on Friday evening, Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service confirmed they were now scaling down the incident.

Though they warned crews would remain at the scene overnight.

Earlier advice urged locals to keep doors and windows shut due to smoke has now been lifted.



Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service said: “We are now scaling down this incident, but will have a presence on scene throughout this evening (Friday).

“Local residents are advised they can resume usual activities and the safety advice below around doors and windows is no longer required.

“We would continue to ask people to stay back from the immediate area to allow us to work and would like to thank the local community for their understanding and support last night and today.

“The fire in Brunel Way, Thetford, continues to burn but our crews’ skilled work throughout the night means we have been able to scale back resources on scene.

“There are now two aerial ladder platforms and five appliances at the site.



“But during the course of the fire we and Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service have had 27 appliances in attendance, supported by officers and specialist vehicles and an extremely busy Fire Control.

“We’d like to thank everyone in the area for allowing us to carry out our work and for following our advice to keep all doors and windows closed due to the smoke.

“Please continue to do this throughout the day today.

“And thank you to all our crews, fire control, officers, crews from Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service and our support staff who have been working on this incident and others in the county since yesterday.

“Although no-one has been injured in this fire, our thoughts are with the business affected and its staff.”



The inferno has been linked to lithium-ion batteries stored at the site.

Incident commander Simon Mason said the majority of the blaze was caused by the volatile batteries, which can ignite and spread rapidly.

He added: “The building is heavily damaged.

“It’s a big open-plan warehouse with lots of different storage areas.

“Unfortunately, because of that open-plan nature, the fire is able to extend across the entire warehouse floor.”



The fallout has also hit recycling services across Norfolk, with tips refusing electrical waste such as fridges, TVs and batteries.

A spokesperson for Wiser said no injuries had been reported and the fire was “quickly brought under control”.

They added: “Safety has always been our top priority.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We are conducting a thorough assessment of the site and reviewing our processes to understand the cause and further strengthen our preventative measures.

“Operations continue across our other facilities, and we are working to minimise any disruption to our partners and customers.”

News.title: The incredible true story of 'Ham the Chimp' who became first ape in space
News.content:
The incredible true story of 'Ham the Chimp' who became first ape in space

Before the astronauts of Artemis II could embark on their historic space mission, the impact and demands of spaceflight were tested on a series of animals - and a chimp named Ham went down in history

View 2 Images Ham the Chimp in the biopack couch for the MR-2 suborbital test flight. On January 31, 1961, a Mercury-Redstone launch from Cape Canaveral carried the chimpanzee more than 640 kilometers down range in an arching trajectory that reached a peak of 254 kilometers above the earth (Image: NASA/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

A chimp helped pave the way for human space exploration - and he survived. The Artemis II mission came to an end on April 10 as the astronauts safely returned to Earth following a historic 10 days of space travel.

‌



But before humans ventured into space, scientists tested the impact and demands of spaceflight on a series of animals. On January 31, 1961, a chimpanzee, known as Ham the Chimp, went down in the history books as the first great ape launched into space. Ham flew aboard the Mercury-Redstone 2 mission, which was part of the US space program’s Project Mercury.

‌



He had been referred to as “No 65” before his safe return back to Earth, where he was then given the name Ham as a nod to the laboratory that trained him for the mission; the Holloman Aerospace Medical Center. Ham doubles as an acronym for the facility.

‌



It’s believed he wasn’t initially named in case the mission failed and he died - officials wanted to avoid the potential public outcry and bad press that would likely ensue if a named chimpanzee lost his life for humans’ pursuit of space exploration.

Before his mission, Ham received hundreds of hours of extensive training over the course of 15 months. He was taught to do simple, timed tasks in response to electric lights and sounds.

Throughout his pre-flight training, he was taught to push a lever within five seconds of seeing a flashing blue light. If he responded correctly, he was rewarded with a banana pellet but if he failed, he received a light electric shock to the soles of his feet.

‌



Many animals were sent into space before him but the decision to send a chimpanzee was due to their similarities with humans. By observing Ham and the impact space travel had on him, scientists were able to deepen their understanding and research into the possibility of humans going into space.

Ham’s suborbital flight lasted 16 minutes and 39 seconds. While aboard, he was supposed to respond to visual stimuli but a valve malfunction led to the Redstone rocket delivering higher thrust than planned.

‌



As on Earth, Ham’s failure to respond correctly to the visual light cues would result in him receiving an electric shock. Unfortunately, due to malfunctions, the chimp was subjected to an excessive 17 g-force of acceleration, as well as 14.7 g during re-entry.

This, in part, contributed to the two shocks Ham received in flight. His first shock came just after the launch but was because of an error in the testing apparatus; the second was due to the lack of response after he experienced 14 g deceleration.

The results of Ham’s test flight led to Alan Shepard’s suborbital flight on Freedom 7 on May 5, 1961.

‌



After Ham returned to Earth, he was in good physical condition overall, but did suffer a small cut to the bridge of his nose, as well as dehydration and a loss of 5.37% of his body weight.

View 2 Images Ham is also known as 'Ham the Astrochimp' after he was launched into space on January 31, 1961 (Image: Marka/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

But the ordeal left him traumatised. He would get stressed and panic whenever his handler tried to put him back in a capsule for photos, and he was unsettled when the press approached him.

‌



A picture of Ham holding the newspaper with the headline “Space Chimp Lives” after his safe return to Earth was shared on Reddit. In the image, Ham can be seen sitting on a long, thin desk in front of a mirror while holding the paper in both hands.

He dons a T-shirt and shorts and crossed one leg over the other, while opening his mouth widely.

Reddit users shared their thoughts in the comments section. One person said: “‘Space Chimp Lives’ is one of the greatest headlines ever.”

‌



Another agreed: “They should use this every time an astronaut returns.”

A third shared: “I’m pretty sure I got to see him at the zoo not long before he passed.”

Not all animal space travel ended with their survival, though. The story of Laika, the dog who was sent into space to orbit the Earth and never return, regularly causes heartbreak across social media when her tragic story is re-shared online.

Article continues below

On November 3, 1957, the little mixed breed, who was found on the streets of Russia, was launched into low orbit on the Sputnik 2 spacecraft after weeks of training which included getting her used to smaller and smaller crates and cages.

She was never expected to survive the mission, being captured and trained before ultimately being sent to her death.

Around this time, little was known about the effects of spaceflight on living creatures, and animal flights were seen by engineers as a necessary and integral step before human missions could take place.

News.title: 'I'm pregnant with my 14th baby at 46 and my hubby's had the snip'
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: 'I'm pregnant with my 14th baby at 46 and my hubby's had the snip'

Natalie Jackson is a proud mum to 13 children - and there's another on the way. She shares what life is like for her supersize family, including a very expensive food shop

View 6 Images L-R back row Oliver, Kiefer, Rhett, Casper, Elliott holding Indy, Taliesin, Seren and mum Natalie. L-R front row Felix, Milo, Jonah, Delia, Kit, Quinn

Happily working part time in Marks & Spencer, Natalie Jackson was entering a new chapter in life. Her first job since 2006, she finally hoped two decades of changing nappies was behind her. But, as a mum-of-13, when she felt a bit peaky, she sensed it wasn’t a bug. Reluctantly buying a pregnancy test, Natalie, 46, says: “I sat on the edge of the bathtub, waiting for the result. Taking a deep breath, I turned it over to reveal the word ‘pregnant 3+’. I sat on the floor and cried.”

‌



Leaving the test on her pilot husband, Oliver’s bedside table, she says: “He was thrilled, like he always is, and gave me a big hug.” Luckily, the kids, like their parents, are excited to meet Jackson number 14 in June. Oliver, 47, and Jackie’s 13 children include their eldest six - Elliott, 19, who is at university and Casper, 18, Rhett, 17, Seren, 15, Taliesin, 14, Felix, 12 - who are at military boarding school. The remaining kids - Milo, 11, Jonah, 9, Delia, 8, Kit, 7, Quinn, 5, Kiefer, 4 and Indy, 3 - live with them in Lincolnshire.

‌



Incredibly, in light of their massive brood, before having children, Oliver was diagnosed with stage 3 testicular cancer that had spread to his stomach and lungs. He had a testicle removed and the couple were warned they may never conceive naturally. Freezing some sperm before his chemotherapy, his treatment finished in October 2004, with tests the following April confirming their chances of conceiving were slim.

‌



View 6 Images Ben Shephard, Cat Deeley, Natalie, Jackson Oliver Jackson, Family Natalie & Oliver are proud parents to 13 children - ranging from 19 to 3 - and have another one on the way this summer! (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

Natalie’s shattered dreams of having four boys were compensated when Oliver got the all clear. Astonishingly, they were due to start IVF when she fell pregnant naturally. She says: “I was gobsmacked.” Aged 26 when Elliott was born, after that, the kids kept coming. Natalie says: “We felt incredibly fortunate. We’ve never used contraception, because we don’t want to.”

Finally, in September 2018, after 10 children, Oliver had a vasectomy. But, two years later, Natalie fell pregnant again with Quinn! She says: “We just couldn’t believe it. People asked Oliver, ‘How do you know it’s yours?’” His vasectomy had reversed itself - which a doctor told them is unheard of. After Quinn came Kiefer and Indy.

‌



Natalie says: “We regretted having the procedure done, so when it reversed itself, it felt like it was meant to be.” But the couple want Jackson number 14 to be their last and Oliver is booked in for another ‘snip.’ Natalie says: “This really will be our last baby.” The family breadwinner, Oliver is a multi-engine pilot and qualified flying instructor with the RAF.

The family receives no benefits and pay tax at the higher rate. As a parent to a baker’s dozen - with another bun in the oven, Natalie says they do get judged. She says: “I was out with the kids when a woman asked if they were all mine. When I said yes, she looked disgusted and walked away. We also get, ‘Don’t you have a TV?’ and Oliver has been asked how many women the children are with. But people can see on social media that we are a happy and hard-working family, who are simply getting on with it. Not affected by the scrapping this month of the two child benefit cap, she adds: “We’re not impacted, but I understand why it’s such a big issue for others.”

View 6 Images Doting mum Natalie, with some of her beautiful brood

‌



With strong ethical principles, as well as financial constraints, she adds: “We use reusable nappies, buy preloved clothes, do meal-planning, and teach the children to be independent and productive members of society.” Once clothes, toys and equipment are not needed, she sells them or donates them to charity.

The couple met in 2000 when they both worked for the RAF - Natalie in air traffic control and Oliver training as a fast-jet pilot. She says: “I liked his work ethic and his drive” They married in Las Vegas in 2005, living in the US for several years. Some children have been born in hospital and some at home. But Natalie particularly remembers a home delivery in a birthing pool in Las Vegas.

She says: “The midwife was reading stories to some of the kids. It was chaos, but lovely.’ Our home births have been especially lovely, because the other children are there. Elliott and Casper have both cut the umbilical cord, which was such a special experience for them. My quickest birth was Indy in hospital at just 21 minutes!”

‌



Running a household of 15 requires military-style organisation - with the kids making their own beds from the age of nine. She says: “We live in married quarters, in armed forces accommodation. We use seven bedrooms, plus a guest room and a music room. Seren has her own room as she’s 15, while the younger girls, who are eight and five, share. The 10 boys sleep in rooms with bunk beds, which they love.”

View 6 Images Christmas is a family extravagansa, Natalie hangs all 13 children’s stockings over the fireplace, serves two large chickens for lunch and encourages the kids to open presents one by one, so everyone can watch

Stressing the importance of making time for her children, Natalie says: “It might be chatting to Delia about the book she’s reading while I’m cooking dinner, or a trip to Waterstones to pick out a new one. With the older ones away, thanks to technology, we’re in constant contact.”

‌



Natalie’s mum has always been there when a baby’s been due, but the couple’s parents aren’t local and they have no regular help. They drive around in a 15-seater minibus and a seven-seater car. They have to call airlines directly to book flights, because of their numbers. But they’ve taken trips across the US, including a three-week road trip from Vegas to Seattle with six children, aged seven down to five months.

Natalie, now a full-time mum, says: “Our summer holiday this year will probably be a week in Scarborough. We love the North Yorkshire Moors. The kids love beach days, and with a newborn something local and familiar is very appealing.” The couple also find time for romance. Natalie says: “We managed three nights away together last year. Just a couple of trips north to see the older children at school and a visit to Chatham Docks for the Call the Midwife tour. “

But Christmas is a family extravagansa, Natalie hangs all 13 children’s stockings over the fireplace, serves two large chickens for lunch and encourages the kids to open presents one by one, so everyone can watch. She says: “We are never lonely. There’s always someone to play with or someone to have your back.”

‌



6 View 6 Images There's never a dull moment in the Jackson household! 6 View 6 Images Natalie is looking forward to her newest arrival

The eldest boys both have girlfriends, but she adds: “If anyone stays over, they’re in the spare room!’ With her baby due on June 18, Milo’s birthday, she adds: “I’m 31 weeks pregnant. I’m very relaxed, even though I have no baby clothes because I’ve donated and sold everything on Vinted!”

‌



Keeping the baby’s sex as a surprise, she adds: “It will feel wonderful to hold a baby again.” The day after her due date, Natalie and Oliver are meant to be collecting the older children from school in Dunblane, Scotland, for the summer holidays. She says: “Ideally the baby will arrive a few days before, so the older ones can meet their new sibling when we collect them.”

Any anxieties she has about being an older mum have been dismissed by her midwife, who “has no concerns.” She adds: “We have no regrets about having such a big family. We love every single one of them.” And being parents to 13, going on 14 kids, has done nothing to dampen their ardour for each other. Natalie says: “We’re the couple that still holds hands, when they’re not full of little ones! The intimate side of our relationship is very important. Like many women, I have moments of insecurity about my body. But Oliver is incredibly reassuring and always tells me he loves me and my body as it is.”

Oliver says: “I feel incredibly lucky and proud of all our children. Natalie and I have always been a team. What I love most is the closeness in our family. I have huge respect for everything Natalie has done to give us our family. To grow 14 children takes an incredibly strong person. Her ability to organise and manage everyday life, events and holidays for a family of our size still amazes me.”

‌



In one week, the family gets through:

56 pints of milk

12 loaves of bread

‌



5 dozen eggs

24 oranges

36 apples

‌



4 punnets strawberries

12 kiwis

6 toilet rolls

Article continues below

And £300 on the weekly food shop

News.title: "Striking is breaking my heart, but I'm £8k worse off - we have to fight back"
News.content:
On the all-women picket line in South Wales, it’s clear health visitor Jo Hyde desperately wants to get back to the families she gives vital support to, in Merthyr Tydfil.

“In 36 years, I’ve never been on strike,” says Jo, 55, who lives in Ogmore, in the Vale of Glamorgan. “We never thought this would happen. But we have to – we’ve tried every other option. We just want to go back to supporting families. We’re all really struggling, we’re carrying a lot of guilt about the people we support – but the aim is to make sure they remain supported in future, by maintaining a good service where people feel valued and respected, and where we can recruit and retain the best people.”

While headlines have been dominated by the national strike by resident doctors – formerly known as junior doctors – who returned to work on Monday, Jo and her colleagues, who work for the Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board (CTMUHB), have been out for seven long weeks.

View 4 Images Health workers at Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board on the picket line (Image: WalesOnline/Rob Browne)

‌



Over 100 health visitors who cover some of the poorest parts of Wales – Merthyr Tydfil, Rhondda Cynon Taf, and Bridgend – have been striking over a banding decision they say has left them £8000 to £9000 per year worse off. “We work in areas of high deprivation,” Jo says. “We are the gateway to so many services. But it’s become very fragmented and unfair. Health visitors aren’t being paid the same across the UK for delivering the same service.”

The health visitors say criteria which is part of the Agenda for Change grading and pay system for NHS staff, has been differently interpreted in different parts of the country. In Scotland, health visitors are Band 7, acknowledging their specialist skills and masters’ level qualifications. Yet in parts of Wales and England they are Band 6 – a vast difference in pay.

The reluctant strikers are all women. “If you put our skills into the NHS job evaluation process, we should be Band 7,” health visitor Melani Smith, says. “Specialist paramedics are Band 7. They are mostly men.”

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham has backed the health visitors’ struggle. “This is an outrageous ploy from a health board to try and avoid paying its essential staff the money they are worth,” she says. This is a significant pay difference that has left our members undervalued and underpaid. They have been left with little choice but to take strike action and have the full support of Unite in this dispute.”

‌



View 4 Images Melani Smith has been with the NHS 42 years (Image: Supplied)

A former midwife from Aberdare, Jenna Terry retrained so she could be a health visitor – a job she loves. With two young children herself, she says she hates the thought of being on strike and is worried sick about the 200 families she works with – but says she and her colleagues have been left with no choice, after being denied parity with their peers in Scotland.

“We can’t believe this is happening,” Jenna, 36, says. “I want to be in this profession for the long-term – I love it – but we have to stand up for ourselves. I want to be able to tell my children, ‘we fought for this’. We need to be treated with respect, and pay does play a part. We’re looking after children, parents, it’s important to society. This is a vocation. I find it hard to speak up but, my gosh, I have to now. We feel so undervalued and ignored.

“It makes my heart break because I know there are all those people struggling, people I help to support.” Like her health visitor colleagues, Jenna is highly qualified. “You now need a Masters-level qualification to be a health visitor,” she says. “I spent five years studying – first to be a midwife, then one year on specialist community nursing then another year, so we’re all highly experienced, qualified specialists.

‌



“We look after big caseloads – mine is 150-200 families, from ante-natal to five years. We are a Jack of all trades. We are the people who make decisions, referrals across education, health, nutrition, mental health. It’s a lot of responsibility, especially around safeguarding, but the banding isn’t reflecting that.

View 4 Images Former midwife Jenna Terry (Image: Supplied)

“In Scotland health visitors are band 7 automatically. We’re doing the same job here in Wales and England, so why are we being treated differently?”

A spokesperson for CTM Health Board said: “The health board has been in discussion with Unite and health visiting staff since a formal dispute was lodged in February 2024. The dispute, at that time, asked for the Band 6 health visitor job description to be updated to reflect the duties of the role, and to re-evaluate the job. A process to review and agree the revised job description took place, facilitated by NHS Wales Employers.

‌



“The job description, which was agreed in social partnership, was re-evaluated, and came out at the same band, Band 6. The job description was issued to health visiting staff and remains in effect. It is important to recognise that the pay banding for health visitors in Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board is the same the banding for health visitors across England and Wales.”

Melani Smith has worked for the health service for 42 years – as a nurse, then a midwife and now a health visitor for 25 years. “My salary has regressed,” the 59-year-old from Bridgend says. “I should be earning more now than I was as a midwife 25 years ago. During my time, health visitors’ responsibilities have increased. We have a lot of responsibilities, a lot of formal expertise, we work in a lot of different areas, and so much of what we do comes from building trust.

“If someone is experiencing domestic violence, is unable to heat their home or doesn’t have enough food they won’t always tell you that outright – we can observe and hear.”

After weeks of taking action in South Wales, next Wednesday, 50 to 100 of the Cwm Taf health visitors will join hundreds of other Unite healthworkers to protest against NHS cuts to jobs and services outside Parliament. It will be a national moment of solidarity for women strikers who have often felt out on a limb.

‌



“I’ve been with the NHS 42 years,” Melani says. “I don’t want to be on strike. But we have no choice. As health visitors we have been undervalued, and we want it put right.”

News.title: Teachers may take strike action after being offered 6.5 per cent pay rise
News.content:
Teachers may take strike action after being offered 6.5 per cent pay rise

Ballot shows teachers are prepared to strike over pay and funding

View 3 Images National Education Union strike action rally in Centenary Square

Members of the UK’s largest teaching union have said in an indicative ballot that they would be prepared to take industrial action to get more funding for schools. More than nine in 10 (90.5%) National Education Union (NEU) members who voted in the indicative ballot said they would be prepared to take industrial action.

‌



However, fewer than half (48.6%) of eligible teacher members voted in the ballot. NEU general secretary Daniel Kebede said: “This government seems intent on attacking our schools. That is why our members have indicated they are willing to take whatever action is necessary to save education.”

‌



The NEU launched the indicative ballot on February 28 asking members if they would be prepared to strike over teacher pay and workload, and school funding. The teaching unions have criticised the Department for Education’s (DfE) recommendation that teachers should receive a 6.5% pay increase over the next three years.

‌



View 3 Images Teachers from the NEU hold a strike rally at the Department of Education in Westminster

The ballot asked NEU members two questions – whether they rejected this proposal, and whether they would be prepared to take industrial action to reduce workload and to get more funding for an above-inflation pay increase. Nearly all (96%) of teachers who responded to the ballot said they rejected the DfE’s pay rise proposal.

The NEU’s national executive will meet next month to decide next steps. Support staff members of the union also voted in an indicative ballot over whether they would be prepared to take industrial action over funding, workload and redundancies.

‌



More than eight in 10 (86.5%) support staff members who voted said they would be prepared to take industrial action, from a turnout of 55.5%. Mr Kebede said: “It is an inescapable fact that schools are running on empty. More than 15 years of real-terms funding cuts have left us on our knees. Resources have dwindled while workload has increased in intensity.

View 3 Images Strike action could disrupt schools

“Retention rates for teachers and support staff are dire – schools are desperately short of teaching assistants and subject specialists. It feels like there is no help coming.”

Article continues below

He added: “To add insult to injury, schools will be given no new money to fund staff pay. This will mean more cuts – cuts to support staff jobs, cuts to subject choices, cuts to basic resources, cuts that damage children’s education.”

Mr Kebede warned at the NEU’s annual conference that many teachers feel their hope in Labour “slipping away”, and said the NEU would deliver national strike action to save school funding if needed. Delegates at teachers’ union the NASUWT’s annual conference also voted for a motion calling for a national strike ballot if the Government does not provide more funding for schools and special educational needs and disabilities (Send) and take action to cut teacher workload.

Teachers got a 4% pay rise for the 2025/26 academic year. This followed a 5.5% rise in 2024/25, and a 6.5% rise for 2023/34 after the NEU went on strike.

News.title: XL bully owner's family abused pensioner's loved ones as he died slowly in hospital
News.content:
XL bully owner's family abused pensioner's loved ones as he died slowly in hospital

Sean Garner, 31, was sentenced to 12 years in prison after his XL bully Toretto mauled and killed John McColl, 84, in Warrington in February last year.

View 5 Images John McColl was mauled to death by an XL bully (Image: CHESHIRE POLICE/UNPIXS)

The family of a man whose XL bully mauled a pensioner to death abused his loved ones on Facebook while he was fighting for his life in hospital.

‌



John McColl, 84, was attacked by XL bully Toretto in Warrington in February last year. Police had to shoot the animal 10 times to bring it under control.

‌



Sean Garner, 31, was sentenced to 12 years in prison on Friday after a jury found him guilty of Mr McColl's death by being the owner of a dangerously out of control dog. A judge described the pensioner's suffering as "quite unspeakable" as he survived for five weeks before finally succumbing to his injuries.

‌



Due to the horrifying nature of his injuries, his devastated family were only able to spend their final moments with him behind a screen. His daughter, Joann Percival, described how she still relives the agonising weeks in which his loved ones continued to visit the gravely ill great-grandad, whose "awful" injuries were so extensive they were unable to see his face.

View 5 Images The dog, Toretto (Image: CHESHIRE POLICE/UNPIXS)

The 57-year-old said: "We went in and we weren't prepared for what we saw. We didn't see a lot, because he was behind a screen. It was just awful. You relive that all."

‌



Mr McColl was barely able to communicate during his time in hospital, only occasionally able to raise his arms as if protecting himself and uttering the word "dog". But despite the advice of doctors, his granddaughter, Kelly Percival, went behind the surgical screen in order to see his face, Liverpool Echo reports.

The 33-year-old recalled: "He resembled nothing of my granddad. I had never seen anything at all like it. To think that a dog had done that, and that dog was around small babies as well, it's just frightening."

View 5 Images Sean Garner, 31, was sentenced to 12 years in prison (Image: CHESHIRE POLICE/UNPIXS)

‌



Mr McColl even underwent a 17-hour operation in a bid to save his life. At the same time, Garner's family and friends were said to have taken to social media in order to spin false narratives and blame the victim of the dog's savage attack. Their claims included that Mr McColl, a retired steel erector originally from Scotland, had entered the garden and let the dog out himself.

His daughter said: "While my dad was fighting for his life, they were abusing us on Facebook and the comments they were coming out with. We were at the hospital with my dad and all they could do was think of lies."

While Garner claimed at trial he had kept the dog inside a locked shed which he alleged Mr McColl had broken into, Ms Percival believes her dad was doing the "neighbourly thing" in entering the driveway of the owner's home, intending to knock on their door and inform the family their dog had escaped.

‌



View 5 Images John McColl's daughter Joann Percival and her daughter Kelly Percival (Image: Eleanor Barlow/PA Wire)

She added: "We went through so many different emotions as a family, anger, hatred. As a family, we know there was no intent there. Nobody would have wanted something like that to happen and I know that. But the fact is that they've shown no remorse, no empathy, no apology.

"If it had been my dog that had done that, I would have been absolutely devastated and I don't know how I would have got over that. We've had nothing apart from lies, blame and abuse off them. It's shocking. Sean Garner knows what happened that night and, unfortunately, he's going to have to live with that for the rest of his life."

‌



Cheshire Police's Detective Inspector Simon Mills meanwhile detailed how some officers who attended the scene on Bardsley Avenue in Warrington required counselling in the aftermath, saying: "In 28 years, these are the worst injuries I've sadly seen to anybody.

View 5 Images John McColl underwent a 17-hour operation in a bid to save his life (Image: CHESHIRE POLICE/UNPIXS)

"I know as an incident, for everybody that attended, and I'm including the neighbours, witnesses, all the attending officers, medical staff, it was just an awful, traumatic incident for everyone involved, right through to surgeons at the hospitals later."

‌



Det Ins Mills added that he had a "lot of respect" for the dignity shown by Mr McColl's family throughout the past year and said: "They've had to endure comments from posts right from the outset, when Garner was first charged, with people taking the side of the dog owner. They've not been able to grieve properly.

"They've had to hold their emotions throughout the trial, seeing him lie at court and then his family making posts online that I don't think are pleasant in any way. They're just victim blaming. I just hope they can move on from this. They can see Garner and his supporters for what they are. But they shouldn't have to do that."

Garner's partner, Lauren Lawler, took to Facebook to say her life had been "ruined" thanks to the actions of the victim who was mauled and ultimately killed by Toretto. In a Facebook rant she said "(her) dogs would still be alive now" if Mr McColl "didn't take it upon himself to go into (her) garden".

‌



Meanwhile during Garner's trial jurors were shown messages in the wake of the attack, which saw him turn to the "Fambo" group chat for advice. His mum, Maureen McGrain, told him: "Say they're Lauren's dogs. She'll get off with a fine and you'll go back to jail." A contact saved in his phone as "R Steph", his sister, sent further messages saying: "I'd say you're minding whatever dogs done it for your mate who's gone Thailand. Don't know who you would say though."

Garner's trial heard that the Crown Prosecution Service had "seriously considered" criminal proceedings against members of the defendant's family who "encouraged him to lie about the circumstances", although, ultimately, "a decision was taken not to charge those individuals".

Sentencing, Judge Brian Cummings KC told Garner: "I am quite sure that you did not take the measures you claimed to have taken. The dog was not kept locked in a shed on the patio. On the contrary, I am quite satisfied that the only obstacle between the dog and the outside world was a side gate which was secured by nothing more than a simple latch.

‌



"That was no sort of barrier for any large dog and was utterly inadequate, more so when you knew that particular animal was unstable, 'missing a few nuts and bolts', as you put it. The measures that you took were so minimal as to be meaningless.

"In all the circumstances of the case, it was eminently foreseeable that the dog would escape from its insecure closure and that it would attack someone and seriously injure or kill them. That is why these animals are prohibited.

"I am quite sure that Toretto had, in fact, previously displayed aggressive behaviour, and you knew that. It is absolutely the position that the incident could have been reasonably been foreseen. You took no measures to protect innocent members of the public."

Article continues below

The judge added: "I cannot accept that you have shown any true remorse. Remorse means being sorry for what you have done, but you have, from the outset, denied any responsibility whatsoever and tried to lie your way out of it. Your expressed concern for Mr McColl and his family is glib and insincere.

"Actions speak louder than words. Your actions involved contesting the incontestable. If there ever was any remorse, it is completely nullified by your offensive lies."

Garner, who was also sentenced for two counts of owning a fighting dog in advance of the trial, nodded slightly as he learned his sentence but otherwise showed no reaction. Supporters in the public gallery were seen to give him a thumbs up as he was led to the cells.

News.title: NHS to contact millions offering another Covid jab
News.content:
NHS to contact millions offering another Covid jab

Free vaccines will be offered to the most vulnerable

View 2 Images Vaccines will be given over the coming month

Millions of older and vulnerable people can now book their spring Covid-19 jabs. Officials stressed that previous immunity against the virus “can wane over time” and urged those eligible to book an appointment.

‌



Tens of thousands of slots a day are now available at GP practices and community pharmacies across England. People aged 75 and over are eligible for the jab, along with older people in care homes and those with weakened immune systems.

‌



NHS England said these patients will be invited to come forward, but they do not need to wait to book an appointment. Slots can be secured using the NHS app, or by going online, visiting a walk-in site or calling 119.

‌



View 2 Images Experts say your immunity may have faded

Covid-19 spreads year round and can be life-threatening to elderly or vulnerable people. Caroline Temmink, director of vaccination at NHS England, said: “With us all experiencing lighter and warmer days, it can be harder to imagine getting sick from viruses like Covid-19, but they do circulate all year and can be just as dangerous for those who are vulnerable.

Article continues below

“Previous immunity can wane over time, so we are encouraging all those who are eligible to come forward as soon as possible to get protected. You do not need to wait for an invite to book you’re eligible – just visit the NHS website, use the NHS App or call 119 to get an appointment in your diary.”

News.title: Brother's brutal eight-word take on bride in black paint attack
News.content:
Brother's brutal eight-word take on bride in black paint attack

Gemma Monk's sister in law carried out a vindictive attack - covering her in paint - in a move that stunned guests just moments before she would marry her partner of 20 years

View 5 Images Gemma Monk was covered in paint following the attack on her wedding day (Image: Cover Images)

A brother unleashed his brutal eight-word take after a bride was left covered in black paint during a vindictive "wedding "revenge" attack.

‌



Bride Gemma Monk, 35, claimed she was subjected to the attack by her sister-in-law which was witnessed by stunned guests who arrived to see her tie the knot with her husband Ken. Antonia Eastwood, the wife of Gemma's older brother Ashley, fled Maidstone's Oakwood House Register Office, leaving the paint-covered bride in tears.

‌



Following the incident her brother Ashley said he had disowned his sister, adding: "We don't want anything to do with her." Thankful, Gemma still managed to compose herself and washed the paint away from her face in a nearby cubicle and used a replacement dress before she married her partner of more than 20 years.

‌



Neither Ashley or Eastwood had been invited to the wedding following a bitter feud that started a year before at their own nuptials. Ashley admitted there had been "disagreements" in the family ahead of the wedding but that he did not want to air them publicly.

View 5 Images Gemma Monk and her husband Ken got married despite the attack (Image: Cover Images)

Coronation Street Lisa and Carla wedding first look as Roy makes moving gesture READ MORE :

He said: "There's more to it. But she’s been punished now, she's suffered more than enough. We want it over and done with." He said: "she's done what she's done" and they now wanted to put it all behind them. He added: "I can't believe it's taken 18 months to get to this."

‌



Gemma spoke following the attack: "We had waited for that day for so long. Nothing was going to stop me. She was determined that the wedding was not going to happen. I did not think twice, I would have walked down the aisle in my knickers and with black paint over my face if I had to."

View 5 Images Gemma Monk spoke out following sentencing at Maidstone Crown Court (Image: Cover Images)

Gemma shared her account after Eastwood, 49, from Manchester, was sentenced at Maidstone Crown Court after she admitted to two counts of criminal damage. The court heard the bill for repairs and "loss of revenue" at the venue was estimated to be in excess of £5,000.

‌



Gemma told the court she had been falsely accused of "trying to trip up" Eastwood at her Dover wedding in September 2023. Relations between the couples have now deteriorated, despite Ken previously being Ashley's closest friend - even introducing him to his sister when she was 14.

Fighting back tears, Gemma delivered her impact statement, adding: "To have paint thrown over me by my brother’s wife changed my outlook on life and made me question whether I had done something really bad, whether I had done something wrong.

View 5 Images Antonia Eastwood on her wedding day

‌



"This has had a dramatic impact on my life. Even while I was providing this statement at the police station, I got extremely emotional and started crying while talking about the incident.

"Since the incident, if it wasn't for my children or my family, I don't think I would even get out of bed to care for myself. I have lost all my dignity and good habits in life. I have lost who I used to be. This has turned the most special day of my life into the worst memory I will never forget, and neither will my family."

Gemma's wedding went ahead on May 24, 2024, two hours after the paint attack at the Victoria mansions, which was temporarily forced to shutdown for clean up work. The mental health care worker said she had battled depression and been left unable to work following the incident.

‌



Prosecutor Pietro Matarazzo told the court: "Her wedding dress turned black. It was splattered with paint, as were her eyes, face, and skin." Gemma recognised her sister-in-law was behind the attack and managed to seize her by the hair but she escaped.

View 5 Images Eastwood was given a restraining order (Image: Cover Images)

The wedding for approximately 50 guests, which included a reception at The Fields at Aylesford, cost around £8,000. Gemma spent £1,800 on her dress, in contrast to the replacement gown, which was too large for her.

Article continues below

A guest at the wedding said: "She was so determined that she wanted her day. She's strong-hearted. When she walked down the aisle with her dad, she did amazingly to hold it all together.

"Everyone started applauding her as she walked down the aisle. You could see a tear in her eye. She's one in a million."

Eastwood was given a 10-year restraining order and ordered to pay £5,000 in compensation - a total of £4,000 to her sister-in-law and £1,000 to Oakwood House.

News.title: Mum's heartbreak as tiny daughter's skin 'burns' and leaves bedsheets 'covered in blood'
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Mum's heartbreak as tiny daughter's skin 'burns' and leaves bedsheets 'covered in blood'

EXCLUSIVE: The 'heartbroken' mum is battling to find out what is causing her tiny two-year-old girl to wake up in the night 'crying' from the painful sores, which leave the bed 'soaked' with blood

View 5 Images A mum has told how her two-year-old 'wakes up crying' in excruciating pain from a mystery illness (Image: Supplied)

A tormented mum has told the Mirror she is desperate for "answers" as her two-year-old daughter battles a painful illness that leaves bedsheets covered in blood.

‌



The exhausted parent, who is from the Stockport area but has asked not be named, said it's "absolutely heartbreaking" to see her little girl struggle "every day" at "such a young age" - and has now started a GoFundMe after trying "everything" to make her better.

‌



In her short life the girl has battled a series of punishing health issues, including hand, foot and mouth disease twice, bronchiolitis, eczema and asthma. She also suffers allergic reactions to many everyday foods, including fruits, vegetables, nuts, and eggs, oats, soya, gluten and dairy, leaving her with very limited food options.

‌



The toddler's problems began at just ten days old, when she became severely unwell. She was diagnosed with breathing issues and put on a CPAP machine. She was given antibiotics and stayed in the hospital for three weeks, but showed little signs of improvement, leading her mum to plead for treatment in the first few weeks of her life.

View 5 Images The toddler regularly breaks out in painful sores and rashes all over her body (Image: Supplied)

Deranged paramedic secretly gave abortion drug to pregnant woman who then lost her baby READ MORE :

The mum said the many trips to the doctor saw her daughter's illnesses "frequently dismissed as viral", despite her baby being prescribed antibiotics multiple times, and she believes she was treated as if she was worrying too much about her child. "On one occasion, I was even asked if I was a first time mum, which made me feel as though my concerns were not being taken seriously", she said.

‌



Then, shortly after her first vaccinations, a rash developed, which doctors attributed to a milk allergy. She was prescribed piriton and prescription milk, but the girl's skin continued to deteriorate, and the itching became constant.

View 5 Images The mum feels her views on what is causing her daughter's struggles are 'not being taken seriously' by doctors (Image: Supplied)

What followed was a ladder of increasingly strong topical treatments, beginning with hydrocortisone and escalating to potent steroid creams like dermavate and protopic, but none seemed to help the poor girl - who by now was waking up in the night crying due to the pain.

‌



The mum explained: "There's been many times our bedding is full of blood. I have spent countless nights rubbing her skin just so she can get some sleep. During the day, she often sleeps excessively due to exhaustion but still we have to rub her skin to help her sleep. When we go out, she frequently reacts to her environment.

"We have tried multiple ways to prevent her from scratching, including sleep sleeves and purchasing a Scratch Star to help ease the urge. Despite this, she continues to scratch even with mitts on and will sometimes use items around the house to try to relieve the itch, which shows how intense and constant her discomfort is."

Alternative treatments, such as Oilatum and oat baths, offered no relief, and even seemed to compound the issues, as her skin reacted to the oats. Eventually, the various treatments took their toll, and she suffered from steroid withdrawal - making "her skin worsen much more and weep".

‌



View 5 Images Countless different treatments have not alleviated her eczema and asthma - and some have made it worse (Image: Supplied)

Alongside the skin issues, the baby faced a barrage of other health battles, including contracting hand, foot and mouth disease twice, suffering numerous bouts of bronchiolitis, and regularly needing inhalers.

At one year old, doctors recommended the girl go on methotrexate - a powerful immunosuppressant used to treat severe psoriasis along with a range of illnesses - but the mum was reluctant, initially agreeing to the treatment before changing her mind over the potential impacts of the drug on her child's already weakened immune system.

‌



Determined to find the root cause rather than just "treat the symptoms", the mum has implemented sweeping lifestyle changes - including changing her daughter's diet, installing a bath filter and humidifier, introducing probiotics, using natural cleaning products, and trying detoxes. Sadly, her condition has not improved.

It's resulted in difficult conversations with doctors, who have tried to impress on her the importance of giving her the drugs they are prescribing.

"I have been told that it could be considered neglect if I do not proceed with medications that I do not feel comfortable giving my daughter - even after the doctor said what an incredible job I had been doing", she said. "As a mother, it's incredibly distressing. Making these decisions is extremely difficult. If my daughter, at just two years old, could understand and be asked whether she wants repeated blood tests or oral steroids, I believe she would say no. Some creams sting her skin, even if she gets in the bath without the filter, it stings her skin."

‌



View 5 Images The mother is now raising money for private treatment (Image: Supplied)

When the mother returned to the doctors to explore alternatives to methotrexate and inquire if gut health could be contributing, she claims she was shut down and bluntly told that eczema is "not related to the gut".

With her daughter now two years old and still in "constant" pain, the mum-of-one is now raising money on a GoFundMe page to find a private specialist who will look beyond "managing symptoms alone".

‌



Away from her daughter's medical battles, the family has also faced a number of difficult personal setbacks. They moved into a new build home with laminate flooring in a desperate bid to reduce environmental triggers, but found it made no difference. She also lost her job somewhere she "truly believed I’d be for life", and felt abandoned by her support network when she needed them most.

Adding to the devastation, after sharing their story publicly, the mum said her and her neighbour's car was mysteriously targeted and its windows smashed.

"Everything has felt like one thing after another", she said, "but I will continue to do everything I can for my daughter."

Article continues below

"We currently park in disabled bays while waiting for a disability badge, as the nearest available parking is around a 15-minute walk away. With frequent hospital visits, often during the night, it is incredibly difficult and unsafe to be walking that distance with my daughter especially when she struggles to walk due to the severity of her skin most of the time."

Speaking of the intense learning process she has had to go through as a mum to a sick child, she added: "I honestly believe I was ignorant to eczema, allergies, and asthma before all of this. But the truth is, unless you go through it yourself or witness someone you love living in that pain every single day, you can never truly understand how much it affects every part of life."

News.content: They also cast doubt on whether Sir Olly ever actually saw the recommendation to the Foreign Office not to approve Lord Mandelson's vetting, saying it was unlikely he was given the full report and may only have seen more specific risks thrown up during the process.

A mother has launched a desperate appeal for stem cell donors to save her two young sons, who are battling a rare and life-threatening genetic disorder.

Marcela Zberea hopes a transplant will offer Cezar, two, and David Nica, 10 months, "a chance at a normal life”.

Both boys have been diagnosed with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS), a severe condition that profoundly compromises the body's ability to fight infection.

Symptoms include easy bruising, eczema, bloody diarrhoea, and prolonged bleeding from minor injuries. The disorder almost exclusively affects boys, with only around three in every million worldwide, due to its genetic link to the X chromosome.

Cezar was just weeks old when he was hospitalised with low blood platelet counts, leading to extensive testing. The devastating diagnosis of WAS for both brothers came during the same appointment, shortly after Ms Zberea, 29, had given birth to David.

"It was so much to take," Ms Zberea recounted. "They were both diagnosed during the same appointment. I had just given birth and David was a newborn in my lap. The doctors told us that a stem cell transplant is their only chance."

open image in gallery Cezar Nica, aged two, has been diagnosed with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS) ( Family Handout/DKMS )

Currently, the boys lead "very restricted lives”, their mother explained, too vulnerable to attend playgroups or interact with other children. Neither Ms Zberea nor their father, Stelian Dorin Nica, 36, are a match for their sons.

The west London family is now collaborating with the stem cell charity DKMS, urging the public to register as potential donors, with a particular call for those of Eastern European heritage.

"I just hope my boys get the chance to live long, happy lives," Ms Zberea said. "Right now, their lives are very restricted and they don’t get to be like normal children. They are too vulnerable to go to playgroup, or have fun with other kids. A stem cell transplant could give them a chance at a normal life."

She added: "We are encouraging everyone to register as a stem cell donor, as anyone could be a match. You could save a life – maybe even one of our boys."

open image in gallery The family is hoping a stem cell donor will come forward ( Family Handout/DKMS )

Bronagh Hughes, a spokeswoman for DKMS, underscored the urgency of the appeal.

"For Cezar, David and so many other patients, the right stranger signing up to the register could be their only hope," she stated. "It takes just a few minutes to register, but it could mean a lifetime for someone else.

“We urgently need more people to come forward, to help give these two young brothers, and others diagnosed with blood cancers or disorders, the future they deserve."

Oil prices dropped back to where they were in the early days of the Iran war, and US stocks raced to another record Friday after Iran said the Strait of Hormuz is open again for commercial tankers carrying crude from the Persian Gulf to customers worldwide.

The S&P 500 leaped 1.2 per cent to an all-time high and closed out a third straight week of big gains, its longest streak since Halloween. A freer flow of oil could take pressure off prices not only for gasoline but also for groceries and all kinds of other products that get moved by vehicles. It could even ultimately help people pay less on credit-card interest and mortgage bills.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged as many as 1,100 points before paring its gain to 868, or 1.8 per cent. The Nasdaq composite climbed 1.5 per cent.

The US stock market has jumped more than 12 per cent since hitting a bottom in late March on hopes the United States and Iran can avoid a worst-case scenario for the global economy despite their war. Friday’s reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, which may only be temporary, is the clearest signal yet for optimism, and president Donald Trump said late Thursday that the war “should be ending pretty soon”.

The price for a barrel of benchmark US crude plunged immediately after Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on X that passage for all commercial vessels through the strait “is declared completely open” as a ceasefire appears to be holding in Lebanon. He said it would stay open for the remaining period of the ceasefire, and the price for U.S. oil dropped 9.4 per cent to settle at $82.59 per barrel.

Brent crude, the international standard, fell 9.1 per cent to settle at $90.38 per barrel. To be sure, it remains above its $70 price from before the war, indicating some caution is still embedded in financial markets.

US stocks are heading toward the end of a third straight week of big gains.

Several times since the war began, optimism on Wall Street has quickly deteriorated into doubt about a possible end to the fighting. That in turn has caused vicious and sudden swings of prices for everything from stocks to bonds to oil.

Minutes after the Iranian foreign minister’s announcement of the Strait of Hormuz’s reopening, Mr Trump said on his social media network that the US navy’s blockade of Iranian ports remains “in full force” until both sides reach a deal on the war. He, though, also suggested that “should go very quickly in that most of the points are already negotiated” and emphasized it by using all capital letters.

Companies with big fuel bills soared to some of Wall Street’s biggest gains following the easing of oil prices.

United Airlines flew 7.1 per cent higher, and Southwest Airlines climbed 5.1 per cent. A day earlier, the head of the International Energy Agency had said that Europe has “maybe six weeks or so” of remaining jet fuel supplies.

Operators of cruise ships, which guzzle fuel, also steamed higher. Royal Caribbean Group gained 7.3 per cent and Carnival rose 7 per cent.

Housing and auto-related companies likewise got some relief from the drop in oil prices.

With less threat of high inflation hurting the economy, a sustained drop in oil prices could convince the Federal Reserve to resume its cuts to interest rates to help the economy. The yield on the 10-year Treasury sank to 4.24 per cent from 4.32 per cent late Thursday, and lower yields can bring down rates for mortgages and other loans going to U.S. households and businesses.

Builders FirstSource, a supplier of windows and other products, rose 5.5 per cent, and homebuilder PulteGroup gained 5 per cent on hopes that lower mortgage rates will spur more people to buy houses. Carvana climbed 7 per cent because lower loan rates can get more customers into new autos.

A strong start to the earnings reporting season for big U.S. companies has also helped support the U.S. stock market, and more financial companies joined the list delivering bigger profits for the start of 2026 than analysts expected.

State Street rose 2.5 per cent, and Fifth Third Bancorp added 1.7 per cent after both reported better results for the latest quarter than expected.

They helped offset a 9.7 per cent slide for Netflix, which fell even though it delivered a better profit than expected. It did not raise its forecast for revenue growth for the full year, which analysts said may have disappointed some investors.

It also said Reed Hastings, cofounder and chairman of the streaming company, will step down from its board of directors in June when his term expires.

All told, the S&P 500 rose 84.78 points to 7,126.06. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 868.71 to 49,447.43, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 365.78 to 24,468.48.

In stock markets abroad, stock indexes leaped in Europe following Iran’s announcement about the Strait of Hormuz. France’s CAC 40 jumped 2 per cent, and Germany’s DAX returned 2.3 per cent.

In Asia, where trading finished for the day before the announcement, indexes were weaker. Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 1.8 per cent, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 0.9 per cent for two of the bigger losses.
